# 19) Threading, CPU pools, IO pools, and performance controls

## 19.0 Chapter contract

Scope: `pa.cpu_count()`, `pa.set_cpu_count()`, `pa.io_thread_count()`, `pa.set_io_thread_count()`, process-level environment controls, per-call `use_threads`, dataset scanner `batch_size` / `batch_readahead` / `fragment_readahead`, filesystem IO, CSV parsing, Parquet reads, dataset writes, compute kernels, table joins/grouping, memory-pool coupling, and production tuning profiles.

Core model: PyArrow inherits Arrow C++’s split between a **CPU thread pool** for CPU-bound parallel tasks and an **IO thread pool** for blocking IO work. Arrow C++ documents that Parquet column decoding is an example CPU-parallel task, while blocking operations belong on a separate IO pool; the IO pool defaults to 8 threads and may benefit from higher capacity on remote filesystems such as S3, while increasing the CPU pool beyond hardware capacity is usually not beneficial. ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 19.1 Threading control surface map

| Control                     | Layer              | Affects                                 | Default / source                  | Runtime mutable                        |
| --------------------------- | ------------------ | --------------------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| `OMP_NUM_THREADS`           | env                | initial CPU pool                        | inspected at startup              | no, env itself not reliable after load |
| `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT`          | env                | initial CPU pool upper bound            | inspected at startup              | no, env itself not reliable after load |
| `pa.cpu_count()`            | Python             | CPU pool capacity observation           | startup env or hardware threads   | read-only                              |
| `pa.set_cpu_count(n)`       | Python             | CPU pool capacity override              | explicit integer                  | yes                                    |
| `ARROW_IO_THREADS`          | env                | initial IO pool                         | Arrow C++ env                     | no, env itself not reliable after load |
| `pa.io_thread_count()`      | Python             | IO pool capacity observation            | fixed at startup unless changed   | read-only                              |
| `pa.set_io_thread_count(n)` | Python             | IO pool capacity override               | positive integer                  | yes                                    |
| `use_threads=True/False`    | per-call           | operation-level CPU parallel scheduling | API-specific default              | yes, per operation                     |
| `batch_size`                | scanner/read/write | batch row cap / memory granularity      | API-specific                      | yes, per scan/write                    |
| `batch_readahead`           | scanner            | per-file read-ahead depth               | default 16                        | yes, per scanner                       |
| `fragment_readahead`        | scanner            | file/fragment read-ahead depth          | default 4                         | yes, per scanner                       |
| `pre_buffer`                | Parquet            | parallel coalesced file reads           | default `True` in `pq.read_table` | yes, per read                          |

`pa.cpu_count()` returns the number of threads used in parallel operations; it is determined at startup from `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT`, or hardware threads when neither is set, and can be changed by `pa.set_cpu_count()`. ([Apache Arrow][2]) `pa.io_thread_count()` returns the number of threads used for IO operations, and the docs explicitly note that dataset scanning implicitly uses this pool and that it can be changed with `pa.set_io_thread_count()`. ([Apache Arrow][3])

---

## 19.2 CPU pool API

### 19.2.1 Observe

```python id="cpu_observe"
import pyarrow as pa

n_cpu = pa.cpu_count()
print({"pyarrow_cpu_threads": n_cpu})
```

`pa.cpu_count()` reports the number of threads PyArrow uses in parallel operations; startup selection inspects `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT`, falling back to hardware threads when neither is present. ([Apache Arrow][2])

### 19.2.2 Override at runtime

```python id="cpu_set"
import pyarrow as pa

pa.set_cpu_count(4)
assert pa.cpu_count() == 4
```

`pa.set_cpu_count(int count)` sets the number of threads used in parallel operations. ([Apache Arrow][4])

### 19.2.3 Deployment use cases

```bash id="cpu_env"
# single worker, host mostly dedicated
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=8
export OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=8

# many workers per host / Kubernetes CPU limit=2
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=2
export OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=2

# CI determinism
export OMP_NUM_THREADS=1
export OMP_THREAD_LIMIT=1
```

Best practice: set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and `OMP_THREAD_LIMIT` before importing PyArrow for process-level defaulting, then optionally call `pa.set_cpu_count(...)` inside the application to make the effective setting visible and testable. Arrow C++ warns that many environment variables are inspected only once per process, so late mutation of environment variables should not be treated as reliable runtime configuration. ([Apache Arrow][5])

---

## 19.3 IO pool API

### 19.3.1 Observe

```python id="io_observe"
import pyarrow as pa

n_io = pa.io_thread_count()
print({"pyarrow_io_threads": n_io})
```

`pa.io_thread_count()` reports the number of IO threads; the docs state that many operations, including dataset scanning, implicitly use this pool, and that the count is fixed at startup unless modified with `pa.set_io_thread_count()`. ([Apache Arrow][3])

### 19.3.2 Override

```python id="io_set"
import pyarrow as pa

pa.set_io_thread_count(16)
assert pa.io_thread_count() == 16
```

`pa.set_io_thread_count(int count)` sets the maximum number of IO threads; the count must be positive. ([Apache Arrow][6])

### 19.3.3 Deployment profiles

```bash id="io_env"
# local SSD / moderate concurrency
export ARROW_IO_THREADS=8

# remote object store scans
export ARROW_IO_THREADS=32

# HDD / low-concurrency embedded box
export ARROW_IO_THREADS=4

# CI deterministic low-noise profile
export ARROW_IO_THREADS=1
```

Arrow C++ documents that the IO pool defaults to 8 threads, should be sized according to IO hardware, and may benefit from a larger size for remote filesystems such as S3 where many concurrent reads can improve throughput. ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 19.4 `use_threads`: per-operation parallelism switch

`use_threads` is not the same as pool size. It is a per-operation instruction: “this operation may schedule parallel CPU work.” Pool size determines how much capacity is available when the operation is allowed to parallelize.

```python id="use_threads_model"
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.dataset as ds
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
import pyarrow.csv as csv

pa.set_cpu_count(8)
pa.set_io_thread_count(32)

# Per-operation CPU parallelism allowed
table = pq.read_table("dataset/", use_threads=True)

# Per-operation CPU parallelism disabled
table_serial_columns = pq.read_table("dataset/", use_threads=False)

# Dataset scan parallelism allowed
dataset = ds.dataset("dataset/", format="parquet")
scanner = dataset.scanner(use_threads=True)

# CSV parser parallelism allowed
opts = csv.ReadOptions(use_threads=True, block_size=1 << 20)
table_csv = csv.read_csv("input.csv", read_options=opts)
```

Parquet `read_table(..., use_threads=True)` performs multithreaded column reads; CSV `ReadOptions(use_threads=True)` uses multiple threads to accelerate reading; scanner `use_threads=True` allows maximum parallelism determined by available CPU cores. ([Apache Arrow][7])

---

## 19.5 Dataset scanner controls

### 19.5.1 Canonical scanner

```python id="scanner_canonical"
import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

pa.set_cpu_count(8)
pa.set_io_thread_count(32)

dataset = ds.dataset(
    "s3://bucket/events/",
    format="parquet",
    partitioning="hive",
)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    columns={
        "event_ts": ds.field("event_ts"),
        "user_id": ds.field("user_id"),
        "value2": ds.field("value") * 2,
        "source_file": ds.field("__filename"),
    },
    filter=(ds.field("year") == 2026) & (ds.field("value") > 0),
    batch_size=131_072,
    batch_readahead=16,
    fragment_readahead=8,
    use_threads=True,
    cache_metadata=True,
    memory_pool=pa.default_memory_pool(),
)

for batch in scanner.to_batches():
    # process bounded RecordBatch
    ...
```

`Scanner.from_dataset(...)` and scanner construction support list or dict projection, filter pushdown, `batch_size`, `batch_readahead`, `fragment_readahead`, `fragment_scan_options`, `use_threads`, `cache_metadata`, and `memory_pool`; scanner filters are pushed down where possible using partition information or metadata such as Parquet statistics, otherwise loaded batches are filtered after read. ([Apache Arrow][8])

### 19.5.2 `batch_size`

```python id="batch_size_profiles"
# low memory / many columns / wide rows
scanner_small = dataset.scanner(batch_size=16_384)

# default-ish throughput
scanner_default = dataset.scanner(batch_size=131_072)

# narrow rows / high-throughput local SSD
scanner_large = dataset.scanner(batch_size=524_288)
```

Scanner `batch_size` is the maximum row count for scanned record batches; docs state reducing it can help when scanned record batches overflow memory. ([Apache Arrow][8])

Value case: `batch_size` controls memory granularity, downstream compute chunk size, Python iteration overhead, cache locality, and latency-to-first-batch.

Deployment advisory:

```text id="batch_size_rules"
Use smaller batch_size when:
  - rows are wide
  - nested columns are large
  - downstream converts to pandas/NumPy
  - memory ceiling matters
  - latency-to-first-result matters

Use larger batch_size when:
  - rows are narrow
  - scan is CPU-bound
  - downstream compute benefits from larger chunks
  - Python loop overhead dominates
```

### 19.5.3 `batch_readahead`

```python id="batch_readahead_profiles"
# minimal buffering
scanner = dataset.scanner(batch_readahead=0)

# default
scanner = dataset.scanner(batch_readahead=16)

# remote/high-latency experimental profile
scanner = dataset.scanner(batch_readahead=32)
```

`batch_readahead` is the number of batches to read ahead in a file; docs warn it may not work for all formats and that increasing it increases RAM usage while potentially improving IO utilization. ([Apache Arrow][8])

### 19.5.4 `fragment_readahead`

```python id="fragment_readahead_profiles"
# low memory / local disk
scanner = dataset.scanner(fragment_readahead=1)

# default
scanner = dataset.scanner(fragment_readahead=4)

# object store / high-latency multi-file dataset
scanner = dataset.scanner(fragment_readahead=16)
```

`fragment_readahead` is the number of files/fragments to read ahead; increasing it raises RAM usage and may improve IO utilization. ([Apache Arrow][8])

### 19.5.5 `to_batches()` vs `to_reader()` vs `to_table()`

```python id="scanner_consumption"
# streaming Arrow batches
for batch in scanner.to_batches():
    ...

# streaming RecordBatchReader boundary
reader = scanner.to_reader()

# full materialization; terminal only
table = scanner.to_table()
```

`Scanner.to_table()` should be used with care because it serially materializes the scan result in memory before creating the table; `to_batches()` consumes the scanner as record batches and `to_reader()` exposes it as a `RecordBatchReader`. ([Apache Arrow][8])

---

## 19.6 Dataset read planning: pool interaction

```text id="scan_interaction"
Dataset scan with use_threads=True:
  CPU pool:
    - decode / filter / projection / expression work
    - column conversion / compute-heavy kernels
  IO pool:
    - file reads
    - remote filesystem requests
    - readahead-driven background reads

batch_size:
  - bounds record batch row count
  - changes memory pressure and downstream chunking

batch_readahead:
  - increases in-file prefetch
  - raises RAM pressure

fragment_readahead:
  - increases concurrent file-level prefetch
  - raises open-file / remote-request / RAM pressure
```

The Dataset API is intended for tabular, potentially larger-than-memory, multi-file datasets; it supports different sources/file formats/filesystems, discovery, predicate pushdown, projection, and optionally parallel reading. ([Apache Arrow][9])

---

## 19.7 Parquet read controls

### 19.7.1 Direct Parquet read

```python id="parquet_read"
import pyarrow.parquet as pq
from pyarrow import fs

s3 = fs.S3FileSystem(region="us-east-1")

table = pq.read_table(
    "bucket/path/events/",
    filesystem=s3,
    columns=["user_id", "event_ts", "value"],
    filters=[("year", "=", 2026)],
    use_threads=True,
    memory_map=False,
    buffer_size=1 << 20,
    pre_buffer=True,
)
```

`pq.read_table(...)` exposes `use_threads`, `memory_map`, `buffer_size`, `filters`, `filesystem`, and `pre_buffer`; `use_threads=True` performs multithreaded column reads, `memory_map=True` uses mmap for path sources where applicable, `buffer_size>0` enables read buffering for column chunks, and `pre_buffer=True` coalesces and issues reads in parallel using a background IO thread pool for high-latency filesystems such as S3. ([Apache Arrow][7])

### 19.7.2 Parquet multithreading value case

Parquet docs state that reading functions use multithreading by default for parallel column reads; depending on IO speed and decode cost, especially GZIP compression, this can yield much higher throughput, and the concurrent thread count is inferred by Arrow and inspectable with `cpu_count()`. ([Apache Arrow][10])

### 19.7.3 `pre_buffer` caution

```python id="pre_buffer_policy"
# Native Arrow S3FileSystem: usually keep pre_buffer=True
pq.read_table(path, filesystem=s3, pre_buffer=True)

# fsspec layer with its own readahead: consider disabling one layer
pq.read_table(path, filesystem=fsspec_fs, pre_buffer=False)
```

The `pre_buffer` docs explicitly warn that if using a filesystem layer that already performs readahead, such as fsspec’s S3FS, disable readahead for best results. ([Apache Arrow][7])

### 19.7.4 Parquet tuning rules

```text id="parquet_rules"
Parquet local SSD:
  use_threads=True
  memory_map=True only if reader/source benefits
  buffer_size=0 or modest
  pre_buffer may be less important

Parquet S3/native Arrow S3FileSystem:
  use_threads=True
  pre_buffer=True
  io_thread_count higher than local default
  project columns aggressively
  filter partitions/statistics aggressively

Parquet fsspec/S3FS:
  avoid double readahead
  choose either fsspec readahead or Arrow pre_buffer
  benchmark both

Parquet GZIP-heavy:
  CPU-bound decode likely
  tune pa.cpu_count()
  avoid excessive io_thread_count if CPU saturated
```

---

## 19.8 CSV parsing controls

### 19.8.1 Multithreaded table read

```python id="csv_read"
import pyarrow.csv as csv

read_options = csv.ReadOptions(
    use_threads=True,
    block_size=1 << 20,
    encoding="utf8",
)

convert_options = csv.ConvertOptions(
    column_types={
        "id": "int64",
        "value": "float64",
        "ts": "timestamp[us]",
    }
)

table = csv.read_csv(
    "input.csv",
    read_options=read_options,
    convert_options=convert_options,
)
```

`csv.ReadOptions(use_threads=True, block_size=...)` controls multithreaded CSV reading; `block_size` determines bytes processed at a time, multithreading granularity, and the size of resulting record batches or table chunks. ([Apache Arrow][11])

### 19.8.2 Incremental CSV reader caveat

```python id="csv_incremental"
reader = csv.open_csv(
    "input.csv",
    read_options=csv.ReadOptions(block_size=1 << 20),
    convert_options=csv.ConvertOptions(column_types={"id": "int64"}),
)

for batch in reader:
    ...
```

The CSV docs state that `open_csv()` is useful for memory-constrained incremental reading, but the incremental reader is currently always single-threaded regardless of `ReadOptions.use_threads`; type inference occurs on the first block and then freezes, so use a sufficiently large `block_size` or explicit `ConvertOptions.column_types`. ([Apache Arrow][12])

### 19.8.3 CSV tuning rules

```text id="csv_rules"
read_csv:
  use_threads=True
  increase block_size for fewer, larger chunks and better type inference
  set column_types for deterministic schema
  use include_columns to reduce parse work

open_csv:
  single-threaded
  streaming / low-memory
  set column_types aggressively
  treat block_size as type-inference sample boundary
```

---

## 19.9 Table operations with `use_threads`

### 19.9.1 Grouping

```python id="group_by_threads"
grouped = table.group_by(
    keys=["country", "year"],
    use_threads=True,
).aggregate([
    ("revenue", "sum"),
    ([], "count_all"),
])
```

`Table.group_by(keys, use_threads=True)` enables multithreaded grouping; when `use_threads=True`, the output ordering is not guaranteed stable. ([Apache Arrow][13])

Deployment rule: if output order is a contract, sort after aggregation.

```python id="group_by_order"
out = (
    table
    .group_by(["country"], use_threads=True)
    .aggregate([("value", "sum")])
    .sort_by([("country", "ascending")])
)
```

### 19.9.2 Joins

```python id="join_threads"
joined = left.join(
    right,
    keys=["id"],
    join_type="inner",
    use_threads=True,
)
```

`Table.join(..., use_threads=True)` performs table joins with an explicit multithreading switch; supported join types include semi, anti, inner, left/right/full outer, and `filter_expression` can apply a residual filter. ([Apache Arrow][13])

Deployment rule: use threaded joins for large relation joins; set `use_threads=False` only for deterministic debugging, extremely small inputs, or thread-budget isolation.

---

## 19.10 Compute kernels and memory-pool coupling

```python id="compute_memory_pool"
import pyarrow.compute as pc
import pyarrow as pa

pool = pa.default_memory_pool()

idx = pc.sort_indices(
    table,
    sort_keys=[("value", "descending")],
    memory_pool=pool,
)

taken = pc.take(table, idx, memory_pool=pool)
```

Many compute functions expose `memory_pool` rather than `use_threads`; for example, `pc.sort_indices(...)` returns stable sort indices and accepts `memory_pool`, while `pc.take(...)` selects values/records and also accepts `memory_pool`. ([Apache Arrow][14])

Agent rule:

```text id="compute_rules"
Direct compute kernels:
  tune allocation via memory_pool where exposed
  tune global CPU pool for operations that internally parallelize
  do not invent use_threads kwargs unless docs expose them

Table-level relational operations:
  group_by(..., use_threads=...)
  join(..., use_threads=...)

Dataset/file readers:
  scanner(..., use_threads=...)
  pq.read_table(..., use_threads=...)
  csv.ReadOptions(use_threads=...)
```

---

## 19.11 Dataset writing performance controls

```python id="write_dataset_perf"
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

ds.write_dataset(
    data=scanner,                       # scanner/reader avoids full materialization
    base_dir="s3://bucket/out/",
    format="parquet",
    partitioning=["year", "month"],
    use_threads=True,
    preserve_order=False,
    max_partitions=1024,
    max_open_files=256,
    max_rows_per_file=5_000_000,
    min_rows_per_group=100_000,
    max_rows_per_group=1_000_000,
)
```

`write_dataset(..., use_threads=True)` writes files in parallel using maximum parallelism determined by available CPU cores; with `preserve_order=False`, multithreading may change row order, while `preserve_order=True` guarantees row order even with `use_threads=True` but can notably degrade performance. The writer also exposes `max_open_files`, `max_rows_per_file`, `min_rows_per_group`, and `max_rows_per_group`; too-low `max_open_files` can fragment data into many small files, and `max_rows_per_file` is the primary file-size control. ([Apache Arrow][15])

Dataset docs additionally warn to avoid files smaller than 20 MB and larger than 2 GB, avoid partitioning layouts with more than 10,000 distinct partitions, and note that Parquet row groups can provide read parallelism and statistics-based skipping but very small row groups inflate metadata overhead. ([Apache Arrow][9])

---

## 19.12 Filesystem IO interaction

```python id="fs_io_patterns"
from pyarrow import fs
import pyarrow.dataset as ds
import pyarrow as pa

pa.set_io_thread_count(32)

s3 = fs.S3FileSystem(region="us-east-1")

dataset = ds.dataset(
    "bucket/events/",
    filesystem=s3,
    format="parquet",
    partitioning="hive",
)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    filter=ds.field("year") == 2026,
    columns=["user_id", "event_ts", "value"],
    use_threads=True,
    fragment_readahead=16,
    batch_readahead=32,
)
```

Filesystem IO is where CPU and IO pools interact most sharply: CPU pool decodes/filter/projects batches, IO pool hides latency and services readahead. Arrow C++ explicitly separates CPU tasks from blocking IO tasks, and recommends sizing the IO pool according to IO hardware, with remote filesystems such as S3 potentially benefiting from many concurrent reads. ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 19.13 Performance tuning profiles

### 19.13.1 Local SSD analytic scan

```python id="profile_ssd"
import pyarrow as pa

pa.set_cpu_count(8)
pa.set_io_thread_count(8)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    columns=projection,
    filter=predicate,
    batch_size=262_144,
    batch_readahead=8,
    fragment_readahead=4,
    use_threads=True,
)
```

Use when storage latency is low and CPU decode/compute dominates.

### 19.13.2 S3/object-store scan

```python id="profile_s3"
pa.set_cpu_count(8)
pa.set_io_thread_count(32)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    columns=projection,
    filter=predicate,
    batch_size=131_072,
    batch_readahead=32,
    fragment_readahead=16,
    use_threads=True,
)
```

Use when latency hiding and concurrent file reads dominate; increase `fragment_readahead` and IO pool cautiously because both increase memory and remote request pressure. Scanner docs explicitly state that increasing batch/file readahead can improve IO utilization but increases RAM use. ([Apache Arrow][8])

### 19.13.3 Low-memory worker

```python id="profile_lowmem"
pa.set_cpu_count(2)
pa.set_io_thread_count(4)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    columns=projection,
    filter=predicate,
    batch_size=8_192,
    batch_readahead=1,
    fragment_readahead=1,
    use_threads=True,
)
```

Use when peak RSS matters more than throughput. Process batches incrementally; avoid `scanner.to_table()`.

### 19.13.4 Deterministic CI / debugging

```python id="profile_ci"
pa.set_cpu_count(1)
pa.set_io_thread_count(1)

scanner = dataset.scanner(
    batch_size=32_768,
    batch_readahead=0,
    fragment_readahead=1,
    use_threads=False,
    cache_metadata=False,
)
```

Use when deterministic logs, stable ordering, and easier debugging matter more than speed. Note: Arrow C++ warns that operations configured for serial execution may still use the IO pool, so “serial” is not the same as “no background IO.” ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 19.14 Measurement harness

```python id="bench_harness"
from __future__ import annotations

import contextlib
import dataclasses
import time
import pyarrow as pa

@dataclasses.dataclass
class Timing:
    label: str
    seconds: float
    rows: int | None
    bytes_allocated_delta: int
    cpu_threads: int
    io_threads: int

@contextlib.contextmanager
def measure(label: str):
    pool = pa.default_memory_pool()
    before = pool.bytes_allocated()
    start = time.perf_counter()
    payload = {"rows": None}
    yield payload
    end = time.perf_counter()
    after = pool.bytes_allocated()
    print(Timing(
        label=label,
        seconds=end - start,
        rows=payload["rows"],
        bytes_allocated_delta=after - before,
        cpu_threads=pa.cpu_count(),
        io_threads=pa.io_thread_count(),
    ))

with measure("scanner_to_batches") as m:
    rows = 0
    for batch in scanner.to_batches():
        rows += batch.num_rows
    m["rows"] = rows
```

Benchmark rules:

```text id="bench_rules"
Always record:
  pyarrow version
  cpu_count
  io_thread_count
  memory_pool backend
  batch_size
  batch_readahead
  fragment_readahead
  use_threads
  filesystem backend
  file count
  row-group/file-size distribution
  compression codecs
  projected columns
  filter selectivity
```

## 19.15 Runtime manifest

```python id="thread_manifest"
from __future__ import annotations

import os
import json
import pyarrow as pa

def thread_manifest() -> dict[str, object]:
    pool = pa.default_memory_pool()
    return {
        "pyarrow_version": pa.__version__,
        "env": {
            "OMP_NUM_THREADS": os.environ.get("OMP_NUM_THREADS"),
            "OMP_THREAD_LIMIT": os.environ.get("OMP_THREAD_LIMIT"),
            "ARROW_IO_THREADS": os.environ.get("ARROW_IO_THREADS"),
            "ARROW_DEFAULT_MEMORY_POOL": os.environ.get("ARROW_DEFAULT_MEMORY_POOL"),
        },
        "runtime": {
            "cpu_count": pa.cpu_count(),
            "io_thread_count": pa.io_thread_count(),
            "memory_pool_backend": pool.backend_name,
            "bytes_allocated": pool.bytes_allocated(),
            "max_memory": pool.max_memory(),
        },
    }

print(json.dumps(thread_manifest(), indent=2, sort_keys=True))
```

Deploy this at worker boot and benchmark start. Thread settings without a manifest are not reproducible.

---

## 19.16 Tuning checklist for LLM programming agents

```text id="agent_checklist"
1. Set process defaults before import:
   OMP_NUM_THREADS
   OMP_THREAD_LIMIT
   ARROW_IO_THREADS

2. Import pyarrow.

3. Apply explicit runtime overrides:
   pa.set_cpu_count(...)
   pa.set_io_thread_count(...)

4. Choose operation-level parallelism:
   pq.read_table(use_threads=...)
   csv.ReadOptions(use_threads=...)
   dataset.scanner(use_threads=...)
   table.group_by(use_threads=...)
   table.join(use_threads=...)
   ds.write_dataset(use_threads=..., preserve_order=...)

5. Bound memory:
   scanner(batch_size=...)
   scanner(batch_readahead=...)
   scanner(fragment_readahead=...)
   process scanner.to_batches(), not scanner.to_table()

6. Avoid double readahead:
   pq.read_table(pre_buffer=True) with native FS
   disable one readahead layer when using fsspec/S3FS

7. Preserve order only when needed:
   group_by(...).sort_by(...)
   write_dataset(preserve_order=True) only under contract

8. Benchmark with actual file layout:
   compression
   row-group size
   file count
   partition count
   object-store latency
```

---

## 19.17 Anti-patterns

* Do not set `OMP_NUM_THREADS` or `ARROW_IO_THREADS` after importing PyArrow and assume process-global pools changed; set env before import or call `pa.set_cpu_count()` / `pa.set_io_thread_count()`.
* Do not use `scanner.to_table()` for large datasets; it materializes the scan result in memory. ([Apache Arrow][8])
* Do not increase `fragment_readahead` and `batch_readahead` without accounting for RAM growth; docs explicitly warn both can increase RAM usage. ([Apache Arrow][8])
* Do not assume `use_threads=False` disables every possible background thread; Arrow C++ notes many operations may still use the IO pool under serial execution. ([Apache Arrow][1])
* Do not rely on grouped aggregation output order when `use_threads=True`; docs say stable ordering is not guaranteed. ([Apache Arrow][13])
* Do not use `csv.open_csv()` expecting multithreaded parsing; docs state the incremental CSV reader is always single-threaded. ([Apache Arrow][12])
* Do not stack fsspec readahead and Parquet `pre_buffer=True` without benchmarking; PyArrow docs explicitly warn to disable one readahead layer for best results. ([Apache Arrow][7])
* Do not set `max_open_files` too low in partitioned writes; docs warn it can fragment data into many small files. ([Apache Arrow][15])

---

## 19.18 Minimal canonical bootstrap

```python id="minimal_bootstrap"
# bootstrap_arrow_perf.py
from __future__ import annotations

import os

# Must happen before importing pyarrow for startup defaults.
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_NUM_THREADS", "4")
os.environ.setdefault("OMP_THREAD_LIMIT", "4")
os.environ.setdefault("ARROW_IO_THREADS", "16")

import pyarrow as pa
import pyarrow.dataset as ds

# Make runtime effective settings explicit.
pa.set_cpu_count(int(os.environ["OMP_NUM_THREADS"]))
pa.set_io_thread_count(int(os.environ["ARROW_IO_THREADS"]))

def scanner_for_service(path: str) -> ds.Scanner:
    dataset = ds.dataset(path, format="parquet", partitioning="hive")
    return dataset.scanner(
        columns=["id", "ts", "value"],
        filter=ds.field("value") > 0,
        batch_size=65_536,
        batch_readahead=8,
        fragment_readahead=4,
        use_threads=True,
        cache_metadata=True,
    )

def run(path: str) -> int:
    rows = 0
    for batch in scanner_for_service(path).to_batches():
        rows += batch.num_rows
    return rows
```

This is the default safe pattern: environment before import, explicit runtime pool sizing, projection/filter at scan construction, bounded batch iteration, no accidental full-table materialization.

# 22) Sparse tensors and dense/sparse numeric containers

## 22.0 Chapter contract

Scope: `pyarrow.Tensor`, `RecordBatch.to_tensor(...)`, `FixedShapeTensorArray`, `SparseCOOTensor`, `SparseCSRMatrix`, `SparseCSCMatrix`, `SparseCSFTensor`, dense↔sparse conversion boundaries, NumPy/SciPy/pydata-sparse interop, memory-layout semantics, table-vs-tensor decision rules, deployment dependencies, and anti-patterns.

The existing draft already frames `Tensor` as the dense n-dimensional branch of PyArrow rather than the columnar/table branch, and warns that `RecordBatch.to_tensor(...)` is a conversion boundary, not the native representation of tabular Arrow.  Current PyArrow v24.0.0 exposes sparse tensor/matrix containers with NumPy/SciPy conversion surfaces, plus fixed-shape tensor extension arrays for tensor-valued table columns. ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 22.1 Numeric container taxonomy

| Container                  | Shape model                                   | Storage model                                   | Row/column names        | Nulls                      | Best use                                  |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- | -------------------------- | ----------------------------------------- |
| `pa.Array`                 | 1-D logical column                            | Arrow buffers + validity bitmap                 | no                      | yes                        | column kernels, schema fields             |
| `pa.ChunkedArray`          | 1-D logical column over chunks                | multiple arrays                                 | no                      | yes                        | table columns, dataset scans              |
| `pa.RecordBatch`           | 2-D tabular batch                             | named equal-length arrays                       | yes                     | yes                        | streaming tabular unit                    |
| `pa.Table`                 | 2-D logical relation                          | named chunked columns                           | yes                     | yes                        | joins, grouping, datasets, storage        |
| `pa.Tensor`                | dense n-D numeric object                      | dense strided memory                            | dim names only          | no Arrow null bitmap       | dense linear algebra / ML kernels         |
| `pa.FixedShapeTensorArray` | 1-D Arrow column, each row fixed-shape tensor | extension array over fixed-size-list storage    | column name + dim names | Arrow array nulls possible | tensor-valued table column                |
| `pa.SparseCOOTensor`       | sparse n-D tensor                             | coordinate/value pairs                          | dim names               | no Arrow null bitmap       | general sparse n-D                        |
| `pa.SparseCSRMatrix`       | sparse 2-D matrix                             | compressed sparse row                           | dim names               | no Arrow null bitmap       | row-oriented sparse matrix                |
| `pa.SparseCSCMatrix`       | sparse 2-D matrix                             | compressed sparse column                        | dim names               | no Arrow null bitmap       | column-oriented sparse matrix             |
| `pa.SparseCSFTensor`       | sparse n-D tensor                             | compressed sparse fiber / prefix-tree structure | dim names               | no Arrow null bitmap       | high-dimensional compressed sparse tensor |

`Tensor` exposes `from_numpy`, `to_numpy`, `shape`, `strides`, `ndim`, `size`, `dim_names`, `is_contiguous`, and `is_mutable`; `to_numpy()` is documented as zero-copy. ([Apache Arrow][2]) Sparse COO exposes constructors from dense NumPy, NumPy buffers, pydata/sparse, SciPy, and dense Arrow tensor, plus zero-copy `to_numpy()`, SciPy/pydata-sparse egress, and dense `to_tensor()` materialization. ([Apache Arrow][1])

---

## 22.2 Selection rule: table vs dense tensor vs fixed-shape tensor array vs sparse tensor

```text id="numeric_container_decision"
Need named heterogeneous columns, null semantics, joins/grouping/sorting/dataset IO?
  -> pa.Table / pa.RecordBatch

Need one dense numeric n-D object, NumPy-compatible shape/strides, no column semantics?
  -> pa.Tensor

Need one Arrow table column whose cells are equal-shaped dense tensors?
  -> pa.FixedShapeTensorArray

Need sparse n-D coordinates/values, arbitrary dimensionality, SciPy/pydata-sparse exchange?
  -> pa.SparseCOOTensor

Need sparse 2-D row-compressed matrix, row slicing / row-major algorithm compatibility?
  -> pa.SparseCSRMatrix

Need sparse 2-D column-compressed matrix, column slicing / column-major algorithm compatibility?
  -> pa.SparseCSCMatrix

Need sparse high-dimensional compressed representation?
  -> pa.SparseCSFTensor
```

Value case: **Arrow tables preserve relational semantics; tensors preserve numeric layout semantics; sparse containers preserve non-zero structure.** Do not force one abstraction into another unless a downstream API explicitly requires that shape.

---

## 22.3 Dense `pa.Tensor`

### 22.3.1 Construction from NumPy

```python id="dense_tensor_from_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

x = np.asarray(
    [[2, 2, 4], [4, 5, 100]],
    dtype=np.int32,
)

tensor = pa.Tensor.from_numpy(
    x,
    dim_names=["row", "col"],
)

assert tensor.shape == (2, 3)
assert tensor.ndim == 2
assert tensor.size == 6
assert tensor.dim_names == ["row", "col"]
```

`Tensor.from_numpy(obj, dim_names=None)` creates an Arrow tensor from a NumPy ndarray; `dim_names` names each tensor dimension. The Tensor docs show the resulting type, shape, and strides. ([Apache Arrow][2])

### 22.3.2 Egress to NumPy

```python id="dense_tensor_to_numpy"
np_view = tensor.to_numpy()
```

`Tensor.to_numpy()` converts an Arrow tensor to a NumPy ndarray with zero copy. ([Apache Arrow][2])

### 22.3.3 Dense tensor diagnostics

```python id="dense_tensor_diagnostics"
diag = {
    "type": tensor.type,
    "shape": tensor.shape,
    "strides": tensor.strides,
    "ndim": tensor.ndim,
    "size": tensor.size,
    "is_contiguous": tensor.is_contiguous,
    "is_mutable": tensor.is_mutable,
    "dim_names": tensor.dim_names,
}
```

Deployment advisory: pass through shape/stride/dim-name metadata when bridging to numeric kernels. Do not treat `Tensor` as a schema-bearing object; it has dimension names, not named fields, field metadata, column nullability, or table-level schema.

---

## 22.4 `RecordBatch.to_tensor(...)`: tabular → dense boundary

```python id="recordbatch_to_tensor"
import pyarrow as pa

batch = pa.record_batch(
    [
        pa.array([1, 2, 3, 4], type=pa.int32()),
        pa.array([10.0, 20.0, 30.0, 40.0], type=pa.float32()),
    ],
    names=["x", "y"],
)

tensor_row_major = batch.to_tensor(
    null_to_nan=False,
    row_major=True,
)

tensor_col_major = batch.to_tensor(
    null_to_nan=False,
    row_major=False,
)
```

Existing draft guidance remains correct: `RecordBatch.to_tensor(null_to_nan=False, row_major=True, memory_pool=None)` is a dense export boundary; supported fields must be integer or floating-point; nulls error unless `null_to_nan=True`; null-to-NaN may promote integer columns to float and lose original column-level typing semantics. 

### Deployment rules

```text id="recordbatch_tensor_rules"
Use RecordBatch.to_tensor only when:
  - all selected fields are numeric
  - output must be dense 2-D
  - field names are no longer required as column semantics
  - null handling policy is explicit

Avoid when:
  - nullable integer fidelity matters
  - mixed numeric/string/categorical columns exist
  - joins/grouping/filtering still needed
  - sparse structure would be more memory efficient
```

---

## 22.5 `FixedShapeTensorArray`: tensor-valued Arrow column

### 22.5.1 Value case

Use `FixedShapeTensorArray` when each table row contains one equal-shaped tensor: embeddings, image tiles, audio frames, model features, covariance matrices, raster patches, vector-valued measurements.

`FixedShapeTensorArray` is not a single tensor; it is an Arrow extension array that can be a `Table` or `RecordBatch` column. PyArrow’s extension docs show creating a fixed-shape tensor type, building fixed-size-list storage whose list size is the product of tensor dimensions, and wrapping it with `ExtensionArray.from_storage(...)`; those extension arrays can be used as table or record-batch columns. ([Apache Arrow][3])

### 22.5.2 Storage-backed construction

```python id="fixed_shape_storage"
import pyarrow as pa

tensor_type = pa.fixed_shape_tensor(
    pa.float32(),
    shape=(3, 4),
    dim_names=["height", "width"],
)

storage = pa.array(
    [
        [0.0] * 12,
        [1.0] * 12,
        [2.0] * 12,
    ],
    type=pa.list_(pa.float32(), 12),
)

tensor_col = pa.ExtensionArray.from_storage(tensor_type, storage)

table = pa.table({
    "id": pa.array([1, 2, 3], type=pa.int64()),
    "patch": tensor_col,
})
```

### 22.5.3 NumPy ndarray construction

```python id="fixed_shape_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

x = np.arange(3 * 2 * 4, dtype=np.float32).reshape(3, 2, 4)

tensor_col = pa.FixedShapeTensorArray.from_numpy_ndarray(
    x,
    dim_names=["row", "col"],
)

table = pa.table({"features": tensor_col})
```

`FixedShapeTensorArray.from_numpy_ndarray(obj, dim_names=None)` converts NumPy tensors to a fixed-shape tensor extension array; `to_numpy_ndarray()` converts the extension array back to a multi-dimensional ndarray. ([Apache Arrow][4])

### 22.5.4 Egress

```python id="fixed_shape_egress"
nd = tensor_col.to_numpy_ndarray()
dense_tensor = tensor_col.to_tensor()
```

`FixedShapeTensorArray.to_numpy_ndarray()` returns a multi-dimensional NumPy ndarray, and `to_tensor()` converts the array to `pyarrow.Tensor`. ([Apache Arrow][4])

### Deployment advisory

```text id="fixed_shape_rules"
Use FixedShapeTensorArray when:
  - tensor values must live inside Table/RecordBatch
  - every row has identical tensor shape
  - table-level metadata/schema/IPC/Parquet flows still matter
  - vector-valued columns should remain one column, not N flattened columns

Avoid when:
  - shapes vary per row
  - sparse tensor values dominate
  - downstream expects SciPy sparse matrix
  - tensor column is only a temporary dense matrix for linear algebra
```

---

## 22.6 `SparseCOOTensor`: coordinate sparse n-D

### 22.6.1 Memory layout

COO stores explicit coordinate tuples plus non-zero values:

```text id="coo_layout"
data:   shape (nnz,)
coords: shape (nnz, ndim)
shape:  full dense tensor shape
```

PyArrow’s `SparseCOOTensor.from_numpy(data, coords, shape, dim_names=None)` creates COO from NumPy arrays; `from_dense_numpy`, `from_pydata_sparse`, `from_scipy`, and `from_tensor` are also documented. ([Apache Arrow][1])

### 22.6.2 Construction from NumPy buffers

```python id="coo_from_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

data = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float32)

coords = np.array(
    [
        [0, 1],
        [1, 0],
        [1, 2],
    ],
    dtype=np.int64,
)

coo = pa.SparseCOOTensor.from_numpy(
    data,
    coords,
    shape=(2, 3),
    dim_names=["row", "col"],
)

assert coo.shape == (2, 3)
assert coo.ndim == 2
assert coo.non_zero_length == 3
```

The official example uses `data = [1.0, 2.0, 3.0]`, `coords = [[0,1], [1,0], [1,2]]`, and `shape=(2,3)` to build `SparseCOOTensor`. ([Apache Arrow][1])

### 22.6.3 Construction from dense tensor / dense NumPy

```python id="coo_from_dense"
dense_np = np.array(
    [
        [0.0, 1.0, 0.0],
        [2.0, 0.0, 3.0],
    ],
    dtype=np.float32,
)

coo1 = pa.SparseCOOTensor.from_dense_numpy(dense_np)
coo2 = pa.SparseCOOTensor.from_tensor(pa.Tensor.from_numpy(dense_np))
```

Use these only when dense materialization already exists or is acceptable. If the upstream data is already sparse, build from sparse buffers or SciPy/pydata-sparse to avoid dense allocation.

### 22.6.4 SciPy / pydata-sparse interop

```python id="coo_scipy_pydata"
# Requires scipy
import scipy.sparse as sp

scipy_coo = sp.coo_array(
    (
        np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]),
        (
            np.array([0, 1, 1]),
            np.array([1, 0, 2]),
        ),
    ),
    shape=(2, 3),
)

coo = pa.SparseCOOTensor.from_scipy(scipy_coo)
scipy_roundtrip = coo.to_scipy()

# Requires sparse / pydata-sparse
# pydata_roundtrip = coo.to_pydata_sparse()
```

`SparseCOOTensor.from_scipy(...)` accepts SciPy COO arrays/matrices, `to_scipy()` returns a `scipy.sparse.coo_array`, `from_pydata_sparse(...)` converts pydata/sparse COO to Arrow COO, and `to_pydata_sparse()` converts back. ([Apache Arrow][1])

### 22.6.5 Zero-copy NumPy egress

```python id="coo_to_numpy"
data_np, coords_np = coo.to_numpy()
```

`SparseCOOTensor.to_numpy()` is documented as converting to NumPy ndarrays with zero copy. ([Apache Arrow][1])

### 22.6.6 Dense materialization

```python id="coo_to_tensor"
dense_tensor = coo.to_tensor()
dense_np = dense_tensor.to_numpy()
```

`SparseCOOTensor.to_tensor()` converts sparse COO to dense Arrow tensor. This can expand memory from `O(nnz * (value_width + ndim * index_width))` to `O(prod(shape) * value_width)`.

---

## 22.7 `SparseCSRMatrix`: compressed sparse row 2-D matrix

### 22.7.1 Memory layout

CSR compresses rows:

```text id="csr_layout"
data:    non-zero values, length nnz
indices: column index for each non-zero, length nnz
indptr:  row pointer, length n_rows + 1
shape:   (n_rows, n_cols)
```

The official docs define CSR as compressed sparse row and say it stores `data` non-zero values, `indices` column indices, and `indptr` row pointers indicating where each row starts in the data array. ([Apache Arrow][5])

### 22.7.2 Construction from NumPy buffers

```python id="csr_from_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

data = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0], dtype=np.float64)
indptr = np.array([0, 2, 3], dtype=np.int64)
indices = np.array([0, 2, 1], dtype=np.int64)

csr = pa.SparseCSRMatrix.from_numpy(
    data,
    indptr,
    indices,
    shape=(2, 3),
    dim_names=["row", "col"],
)
```

`SparseCSRMatrix.from_numpy(data, indptr, indices, shape, dim_names=None)` creates CSR from NumPy ndarrays; the docs state `indptr[i]` to `indptr[i+1]` spans the values in row `i`, and `indices` gives column indices. ([Apache Arrow][5])

### 22.7.3 SciPy interop

```python id="csr_scipy"
import scipy.sparse as sp

scipy_csr = sp.csr_array(
    (data, indices, indptr),
    shape=(2, 3),
)

csr = pa.SparseCSRMatrix.from_scipy(scipy_csr)
scipy_roundtrip = csr.to_scipy()
```

`SparseCSRMatrix.from_scipy(...)` converts SciPy CSR arrays/matrices, `to_scipy()` converts to `scipy.sparse.csr_array`, and `to_numpy()` converts to NumPy ndarrays with zero copy. ([Apache Arrow][5])

### 22.7.4 When CSR is preferable

```text id="csr_use"
Prefer CSR when:
  - matrix is 2-D
  - row slicing / row iteration dominates
  - ML feature matrix is samples x features
  - algorithm consumes scipy.sparse.csr_array
  - storage should avoid duplicated row coordinate per non-zero

Avoid CSR when:
  - column slicing dominates
  - tensor rank > 2
  - coordinate updates/incremental construction dominate
```

---

## 22.8 `SparseCSCMatrix`: compressed sparse column 2-D matrix

### 22.8.1 Memory layout

CSC compresses columns:

```text id="csc_layout"
data:    non-zero values, length nnz
indices: row index for each non-zero, length nnz
indptr:  column pointer, length n_cols + 1
shape:   (n_rows, n_cols)
```

The official docs define CSC as compressed sparse column and state it uses `data`, `indices` row indices, and `indptr` column pointers; CSC is the transpose of CSR format. ([Apache Arrow][6])

### 22.8.2 Construction from NumPy buffers

```python id="csc_from_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

data = np.array([1.0, 3.0, 2.0], dtype=np.float64)
indptr = np.array([0, 1, 2, 3], dtype=np.int64)
indices = np.array([0, 1, 0], dtype=np.int64)

csc = pa.SparseCSCMatrix.from_numpy(
    data,
    indptr,
    indices,
    shape=(2, 3),
    dim_names=["row", "col"],
)
```

`SparseCSCMatrix.from_numpy(data, indptr, indices, shape, dim_names=None)` creates CSC from NumPy ndarrays; docs list `from_scipy`, `from_tensor`, zero-copy `to_numpy`, `to_scipy`, and `to_tensor`. ([Apache Arrow][6])

### 22.8.3 SciPy interop

```python id="csc_scipy"
import scipy.sparse as sp

scipy_csc = sp.csc_array(
    (data, indices, indptr),
    shape=(2, 3),
)

csc = pa.SparseCSCMatrix.from_scipy(scipy_csc)
scipy_roundtrip = csc.to_scipy()
```

`SparseCSCMatrix.from_scipy(...)` accepts SciPy CSC arrays/matrices; `to_scipy()` returns a SciPy CSC array. ([Apache Arrow][6])

### 22.8.4 When CSC is preferable

```text id="csc_use"
Prefer CSC when:
  - matrix is 2-D
  - column slicing / column aggregation dominates
  - downstream algorithm expects scipy.sparse.csc_array
  - feature-major operations dominate

Avoid CSC when:
  - row iteration dominates
  - sample-major ML algorithms expect CSR
  - tensor rank > 2
```

---

## 22.9 `SparseCSFTensor`: compressed sparse fiber n-D tensor

### 22.9.1 Memory layout

CSF generalizes CSR to n-D tensors. The docs state CSF recursively compresses each tensor dimension into prefix trees; each root-to-leaf path forms one non-zero index, and the implementation uses arrays of buffers plus integers. ([Apache Arrow][7])

```text id="csf_layout"
data:
  non-zero values, length nnz

indices:
  list[np.ndarray]
  node values per dimension / compressed prefix-tree level

indptr:
  list[np.ndarray]
  child-range pointers between adjacent dimensions

axis_order:
  traversal order for prefix-tree construction

shape:
  full dense tensor shape
```

### 22.9.2 Construction from NumPy buffers

```python id="csf_from_numpy"
import numpy as np
import pyarrow as pa

data = np.array([1.0, 2.0], dtype=np.float32)

indptr = [
    np.array([0, 1, 2], dtype=np.int64),
    np.array([0, 1, 2], dtype=np.int64),
]

indices = [
    np.array([0, 1], dtype=np.int64),
    np.array([1, 2], dtype=np.int64),
    np.array([0, 1], dtype=np.int64),
]

csf = pa.SparseCSFTensor.from_numpy(
    data,
    indptr,
    indices,
    shape=(2, 3, 2),
    axis_order=None,
    dim_names=["x", "y", "z"],
)
```

`SparseCSFTensor.from_numpy(data, indptr, indices, shape, axis_order=None, dim_names=None)` creates CSF from NumPy ndarrays; the docs describe `indptr` as the sparsity structure between dimensions, `indices` as node values, and `axis_order` as traversal order. ([Apache Arrow][7])

### 22.9.3 Dense boundary

```python id="csf_dense_boundary"
csf_from_dense = pa.SparseCSFTensor.from_dense_numpy(dense_np)
csf_from_tensor = pa.SparseCSFTensor.from_tensor(pa.Tensor.from_numpy(dense_np))

dense_tensor = csf.to_tensor()
data_np, indptr_np, indices_np = csf.to_numpy()
```

`SparseCSFTensor.from_dense_numpy`, `from_tensor`, zero-copy `to_numpy`, and dense `to_tensor` are documented. ([Apache Arrow][7])

### 22.9.4 When CSF is preferable

```text id="csf_use"
Prefer CSF when:
  - tensor rank > 2
  - sparsity is structured across dimensions
  - compressed multi-dimensional traversal matters
  - COO coordinate duplication is too expensive
  - downstream understands CSF or Arrow sparse tensor semantics

Avoid CSF when:
  - downstream expects SciPy 2-D matrices
  - simple coordinate construction/append dominates
  - rank is only 2 and CSR/CSC algorithm compatibility matters
```

---

## 22.10 Interop dependency matrix

| Operation                                                      | Required Python dependency | Arrow class               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------: | ------------------------- |
| `Tensor.from_numpy`, `Tensor.to_numpy`                         |                    `numpy` | `pa.Tensor`               |
| `SparseCOOTensor.from_numpy`, `to_numpy`                       |                    `numpy` | COO                       |
| `SparseCOOTensor.from_dense_numpy`                             |                    `numpy` | COO                       |
| `SparseCSRMatrix.from_numpy`, `to_numpy`                       |                    `numpy` | CSR                       |
| `SparseCSCMatrix.from_numpy`, `to_numpy`                       |                    `numpy` | CSC                       |
| `SparseCSFTensor.from_numpy`, `to_numpy`                       |                    `numpy` | CSF                       |
| `SparseCOOTensor.from_scipy`, `to_scipy`                       |                    `scipy` | COO                       |
| `SparseCSRMatrix.from_scipy`, `to_scipy`                       |                    `scipy` | CSR                       |
| `SparseCSCMatrix.from_scipy`, `to_scipy`                       |                    `scipy` | CSC                       |
| `SparseCOOTensor.from_pydata_sparse`, `to_pydata_sparse`       |   `sparse` / pydata-sparse | COO                       |
| `FixedShapeTensorArray.from_numpy_ndarray`, `to_numpy_ndarray` |                    `numpy` | fixed-shape tensor column |

Deployment rule: list `numpy`, `scipy`, and `sparse` explicitly in environment manifests only when corresponding conversion paths are used. Do not generate SciPy-dependent code paths under a pure PyArrow/NumPy install.
